intro: Writings from the first Christian generations after the apostles: a church manual, letters from bishops and martyrs, the account of a martyrdom, and a defence of the faith. They are not Scripture: the Church never received them into the canon, though some were read in churches early on. But they show what the first Christians believed and how they prayed, and the Church holds them in honour. Several were written by saints, and some by men who knew the apostles.
translation: The translations are those of the Ante-Nicene Christian Library (Edinburgh, 1867–1872) as reissued in the American Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885–1886), in the public domain, as transcribed by the Historical Christian Faith project. Their English is of its time. Words in square brackets were added by the translators to complete the sense.

entries.title: The Didache
entries.subtitle: The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
entries.author: Unknown
entries.date: Probably the late first century, perhaps AD 70–100, though some date parts earlier or later.
entries.about: A short handbook of Christian life and worship, perhaps from Syria. It opens with the “two ways”, one of life and one of death, then teaches how to baptise (in running water if possible), to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times a day, and to give thanks over the cup and the bread. It tells Christians to gather on the Lord’s Day, confessing their sins “that your sacrifice may be pure”, and to choose bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord. Lost for centuries, it was found in a manuscript at Constantinople in 1873. Saint Athanasius recommended it to those preparing for baptism, while placing it outside the canon.

entries.title: Letter to the Corinthians
entries.subtitle: Saint Clement of Rome
entries.author: Written in the name of the church of Rome; from the second century it has been known as the letter of Saint Clement, its bishop, the third after Saint Peter in the list given by Saint Irenaeus (feast 23 November)
entries.date: Usually dated about AD 96; some date it earlier.
entries.about: When some in the church at Corinth deposed their presbyters, the church of Rome wrote to call them back to peace. Clement, its bishop, writes at length on humility, repentance, order and love, with many examples from the Old Testament and a famous passage on the deaths of Peter and Paul (chapter 5). He teaches that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons, and gave instructions that “other approved men should succeed them in their ministry” (chapter 44). Decades later the Corinthians still read the letter aloud in their assemblies.
entries.note: This translation was made from the one manuscript then known, which has lost a leaf near the end. The passage it lacks, including a great prayer for all people and for rulers (chapters 59 to 61 in modern editions), was recovered from a manuscript found in 1873, and the chapter numbers here run differently from modern editions near the end.

entries.title: The Letters of Ignatius
entries.subtitle: Saint Ignatius of Antioch
entries.author: Saint Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, put to death in Rome (feast 17 October)
entries.date: Traditionally about AD 107–110, under the emperor Trajan; some scholars date them later.
entries.about: Arrested in Antioch, Ignatius was taken under guard across Asia Minor to Rome, to die in the arena. On the way he wrote seven letters: from Smyrna to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles and Rome, and from Troas to Philadelphia, to Smyrna and to its bishop Polycarp. They burn with love of Christ and longing for martyrdom, and they are the first writings to speak of “the Catholic Church”. They show churches led by a bishop, with presbyters and deacons. They hold the Eucharist to be the flesh of Christ, and plead for unity around the one altar and the one bishop.
entries.note: The letters survive in a shorter form and a longer one padded out in the fourth century, along with letters falsely given his name. The shorter form, accepted by most scholars as his own, is the one given here.

works.title: To the Ephesians
works.about: Written from Smyrna. Christ is the one Physician, “God existing in flesh” (chapter 7), and the virginity of Mary, her child-bearing and the Lord’s death are “three mysteries of renown” hidden from the prince of this world (chapter 19).

entries.title: Letter to the Philippians
entries.subtitle: Saint Polycarp of Smyrna
entries.author: Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, who as a young man had known the apostle John, according to Saint Irenaeus (feast 23 February)
entries.date: Probably soon after Ignatius passed through Smyrna, about AD 110; some date part of it later.
entries.about: The Philippians had asked Polycarp for a word of counsel and for copies of Ignatius’ letters. He answers simply, weaving in the words of the Gospels and of Saint Paul and Saint Peter: serve God in fear and truth, flee the love of money, care for widows and the sick, pray for rulers and even for enemies. A presbyter at Philippi, Valens, had fallen into avarice, and Polycarp asks them to call him back rather than count him an enemy.

entries.title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
entries.subtitle: The church of Smyrna
entries.author: The church at Smyrna, writing to the church at Philomelium
entries.date: Within a year of his death, which is usually dated about AD 155 or 156, though some put it in the 160s.
entries.about: The oldest account of a Christian martyrdom after those in the New Testament. Old Polycarp is hunted down, brought before the crowd in the stadium, and told to curse Christ. He answers: “Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?” (chapter 9). Afterwards the church gathers his bones, “more precious than the most exquisite jewels”, and resolves to keep the day of his martyrdom each year (chapter 18), the first witness to the Church’s honouring of martyrs and their relics.

entries.title: Letter to Diognetus
entries.subtitle: An unknown Christian
entries.author: Unknown
entries.date: Probably the second century; estimates range from about AD 130 to 200.
entries.about: A Christian explains the faith to an educated pagan who asked who the Christians are and why they appeared so late. Its fifth and sixth chapters, read in the Church’s Office of Readings, describe Christians who live in their own countries as sojourners, obey the laws and surpass them by their lives: “what the soul is in the body, that are Christians in the world” (chapter 6). It survived in a single manuscript, destroyed by fire in 1870.
entries.note: The last two chapters are thought to come from another work by a different hand, and are marked as an addition.

entries.title: The First Apology
entries.subtitle: Saint Justin Martyr
entries.author: Saint Justin, a philosopher from Samaria who found Christ and taught in Rome, beheaded there with companions about AD 165 (feast 1 June)
entries.about: A defence of the Christians addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius: they are not atheists or criminals, and should not be punished for a name. Justin explains the faith to pagan readers, from the prophecies fulfilled in Christ to the moral life of Christians. Its last chapters, 61 to 67, give the oldest full account of baptism and of the Sunday Eucharist: the readings, the homily, the prayers, the offering of bread and of wine mixed with water, the thanksgiving and the “Amen” of the people, and Holy Communion, which is not common bread but the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.
entries.note: Justin ends by adding the emperor Hadrian’s rescript to Minucius Fundanus, which Eusebius also preserves and most scholars accept as genuine; it is given after chapter 68. Older editions print two more letters, said to be from Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius; these are later forgeries and are left out.
